claim: Rotavirus genomes comprise eleven double-stranded RNA segments that are co-packaged into each infectious virion.
source: Genomes of rotaviruses (RVs), and other pathogens of the Reoviridae family, comprise nine to twelve double-stranded (ds)RNA segments, co-packaged into each infectious virion.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Introduction section of the manuscript.

claim: RNA assortment in rotaviruses occurs within cytoplasmic inclusion bodies termed viroplasms.
source: The RNA assortment process, during which a single distinct positive-sense ssRNA copy of each of the genomic segments is selected for packaging and replication, occurs within cytoplasmic inclusion bodies termed viroplasms (Patton and Spencer, 2000; Trask et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research (Patton and Spencer, 2000; Trask et al., 2012).

claim: NSP2 and NSP5 are essential components of viroplasms.
source: Multiple copies of viral RNAs and proteins accumulate in viroplasms, of which the non-structural ssRNA-binding proteins NSP2 & NSP5 are essential components (Patton and Spencer, 2000; Trask et al., 2012; Taraporewala and Patton, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Current views suggest that selection of correct genomic segments is governed by inter-segment RNA-RNA interactions.
source: Current views of the mechanisms of segment assortment are based on the idea that selection of the correct genomic segments is governed by inter-segment RNA-RNA interactions (Gavazzi et al., 2013a; Gavazzi et al., 2013b; Fajardo et al., 2015; McDonald et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: A full set of eleven genomic ssRNAs does not associate into a higher order RNA complex in the absence of NSP2.
source: A full set of S1-S11 ssRNAs does not associate into a higher order RNA complex (cross-correlation function amplitude, CCF ≈ 0, shown as a dashed magenta line).
evidence: This claim is supported by FCCS data shown in Figure 1A, where the CCF amplitude is approximately zero in the absence of NSP2.

claim: Incubation of eleven genomic ssRNAs with NSP2 results in strong interaction between S10 and S11.
source: In contrast, incubation of the mixture of all eleven genomic ssRNAs in the presence of NSP2 results in a strong interaction between S10 and S11 (high amplitude of CCF shown in blue).
evidence: This claim is supported by FCCS data shown in Figure 1A, where the CCF amplitude is high in the presence of NSP2.

claim: S11 RNA preferentially binds to segments S3, S5, and S6 in the presence of NSP2.
source: The strongest pairwise interactions of S11 were observed for segments S3, S6 and S5, with CCF amplitudes similar to those, observed for the S11:S10 complex, incubated in the presence of S1-S9 RNAs (CCFs ~ 0.5, Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by FCCS data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: NSP2 binding to ssRNAs results in structural reorganization of RNA.
source: We show that binding of the rotavirus-encoded non-structural protein NSP2 to viral ssRNAs results in the remodeling of RNA, which is conducive to formation of stable inter-segment contacts.
evidence: This claim is stated in the Abstract and supported by RNA-RNA SELEX data and CD spectroscopy.

claim: NSP5 binding to ssRNAs does not promote formation of stable S5:S11 RNA complex.
source: Despite its ssRNA-binding activity, incubation of NSP5 with ssRNAs S5 and S11 at saturating amounts did not yield any detectable cross-correlation (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B), indicating that NSP5 binding to ssRNAs did not promote the formation of a stable S5:S11 RNA complex.
evidence: This claim is supported by FCCS data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B.

claim: Co-incubation of NSP2 with sub-micromolar amounts of NSP5 results in decreased S5:S11 CCF amplitude.
source: Remarkably, co-incubation of NSP2 in the presence of sub-micromolar amounts of NSP5 resulted in a marked decrease of the S5:S11 CCF amplitude, compared to the NSP2 incubation alone (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by FCCS data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3C.

claim: Addition of 1 mM ATP does not affect RNA binding by NSP2 octamers.
source: Addition of 1 mM ATP did not affect RNA binding by NSP2 octamers (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A), nor had it any effect on the apparent S11:S5 CCF amplitude (Figure 1—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by FCCS data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: Inter-segment RNA contact formation is not coupled to ATP hydrolysis.
source: Collectively these data suggest that inter-segment RNA contact formation is not coupled to ATP hydrolysis and thus most likely to be dependent on the ssRNA-binding activity of NSP2.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the ATP addition experiments showing no effect on RNA-RNA interactions.

claim: C-terminally truncated NSP2 mutant (ΔC-NSP2) has significantly reduced affinity for ssRNA.
source: To further investigate this, we examined the interactions between S5 and S11 RNAs co-incubated with a C-terminally truncated NSP2 mutant (ΔC-NSP2) with a significantly reduced affinity for ssRNA (Hu et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research (Hu et al., 2012).

claim: ΔC-NSP2 shows reduced efficiency in promoting S5:S11 RNA-RNA interactions compared to full-length NSP2.
source: However, the apparent CCF amplitude between S5 and S11 was significantly reduced when the full-length NSP2 was replaced with ΔC-NSP2 (Figure 1—figure supplement 5A, CCFs in blue and magenta).
evidence: This claim is supported by FCCS data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5A.

claim: Rotavirus group C NSP2 cannot substitute for rotavirus group A NSP2 in promoting inter-segment RNA-RNA contacts.
source: A drastic reduction of the CCF amplitude between S5 and S11 ssRNAs was also observed when rotavirus group A NSP2 was substituted with NSP2 from rotavirus group C (Figure 1—figure supplement 5B), despite the apparent structural resemblance and similar enzymatic activities of both proteins (Hu et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by FCCS data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5B.

claim: Inter-segment interactions remain stable after removal of NSP2 by proteinase K digestion.
source: These highly diluted NSP2-free RNA-RNA complexes remained stable at 37°C for extended periods of time (>30 min, Figure 1—figure supplement 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by FCCS data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 6A after proteinase K treatment.

claim: Heat-annealed S11 and S5 RNAs strongly interact with each other.
source: As a further control, we made a protein-free RNA-RNA complex S11:S5 by heat-annealing a mixture of fluorescently labeled RNAs S11 and S5 (Materials and methods), and examined it by FCCS. Both heat-annealed RNAs strongly interacted (Figure 1—figure supplement 6B), yielding an apparent Rh ~13–17 nm typical for a proteinase K-digested complex S11:S5 (Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by FCCS data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 6B and Table 1.

claim: Inter-segment interactions are mediated by direct RNA-RNA contacts rather than protein-mediated bridging.
source: Together, these data strongly support the view that inter-segment interactions mediated by binding of NSP2 remain stable after removal of NSP2 due to the formation of new, specific inter-molecular RNA contacts.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the stability of RNA-RNA complexes after NSP2 removal.

claim: RNA-RNA SELEX reveals multiple areas of S11 RNA undergoing conformational rearrangements upon NSP2 binding.
source: The results of RNA-RNA SELEX against S11 reveal multiple areas of the RNA undergoing conformational rearrangements upon NSP2 binding, while the most stable S11 intra-molecular helices H1-H3 remain largely inaccessible.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-RNA SELEX data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The conserved helices H1-H3 in S11 RNA remain stable upon NSP2 binding.
source: The overall architecture of S11, including stable helices H1-H3, was not affected by NSP2 binding (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-RNA SELEX data shown in Figure 2B and C.

claim: NSP2 binding to S11 RNA results in destabilization of RNA secondary structure as shown by circular dichroism spectroscopy.
source: A positive 260–265 nm band decreases in response to increasing amounts of NSP2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B, shown in blue), or thermal melting (shown in red), indicating that the global helical RNA fold is destabilized by NSP2 binding, consistent with the structural rearrangements due to NSP2-mediated RNA unfolding.
evidence: This claim is supported by CD spectroscopy data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Sequences within S3, S5, and S6 RNAs can stably base-pair with S11 RNA with free energy changes ranging from -15.3 to -19.1 kcal/mol.
source: The identified sequences within S3, S5 and S6 RNAs can stably base-pair with S11 RNA (ΔG = −15.3 to −19.1 kcal/mol, Figure 3, insets and Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by thermodynamic calculations shown in Figure 3 insets.

claim: Mutations disrupting inter-molecular base-pairing between S11 and S5 result in dramatic reduction of CCF amplitude.
source: Substitution of either RNAs with its mutated counterpart (S11mut or S5mut) resulted in a dramatic reduction of the CCF amplitude (Figure 4A, red and blue dotted lines), while the wild-type S5 and S11 RNAs formed stable complexes in the presence of NSP2 (Figure 4A, solid green line).
evidence: This claim is supported by FCCS data shown in Figure 4A with mutated RNAs.

claim: The melting temperature of the S5:S11 RNA complex is approximately 47°C.
source: The FCCS analysis of the preformed S5:S11 RNA complex, incubated at elevated temperatures, yielded the estimated melting temperature, Tm ~ 47°C (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by temperature melting experiments shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Trans-complementary mutant RNAs S5mut and comp_mutS11 strongly interact with each other upon incubation with NSP2.
source: The resulting mutated trans-complementary RNAs S5mut and comp_mutS11 strongly interacted with each other upon incubation with NSP2 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by FCCS data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The CCF amplitude between trans-complementary mutant RNAs is higher than that of wild-type RNA sequences.
source: Moreover, the CCF amplitude between the trans-complementary mutant RNAs was higher than that of the interacting wild-type RNA sequences, consistent with the increased stability of the rescued RNA-RNA contacts (Figure 4—figure supplements 1B, –18.8 kcal/mol for the S5:S11 complex and −23.7 kcal/mol for S5mut:S11comp).
evidence: This claim is supported by FCCS data and thermodynamic calculations shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Sequence-specific inter-molecular base-pairing mediated by NSP2 binding governs inter-segment interactions in rotaviruses.
source: Collectively, our data provide extensive experimental evidence that sequence-specific inter-molecular base-pairing mediated by NSP2 binding to viral ssRNAs, governs inter-segment interactions in RVs.
evidence: This claim is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental results presented in the manuscript.

claim: NSP2 has high affinity for ssRNA but not dsRNA.
source: This model is consistent with the high affinity of NSP2 for ssRNA, but not dsRNA, which may underlie the protein's ability to alter the kinetics of RNA-RNA hybridization by accelerating the breakdown of weaker intra-molecular helices, concomitant with the stabilization of the alternative, stable inter-molecular contacts.
evidence: This claim is based on known properties of NSP2 and is used to explain the observed RNA remodeling.

claim: NSP2 inhibits the initiation of replication but not the elongation stage.
source: Given that NSP2 inhibits the initiation of replication, but not the elongation stage (Vende et al., 2003), it is possible that the inner core protein VP2 binding to the ssRNA-NSP2 complex (Guglielmi et al., 2010; Estrozi et al., 2013; Patton, 1996) would result in the initial displacement of the NSP2 during the core assembly nucleation, followed by further eviction of NSP2 during the elongation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The majority of RNA-RNA interaction sites are located within the coding regions of RV genomic segments.
source: Our data suggest that the majority of RNA-RNA interaction sites are also located within the coding regions of the RV genomic segments (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by the mapping of interaction sites shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: Rotavirus group C NSP2 fails to substitute group A RV NSP2 during assembly of viroplasms.
source: Previously, using a NSP2 complementation system Taraporewala et al. reported that group C NSP2 could not rescue replication in NSP2-deficient cells infected with group A RV (Taraporewala et al., 2006). Our assays present additional evidence that despite multiple structural similarities and analogous enzymatic activities, group C RV NSP2 not only fails to substitute group A RV NSP2 during assembly of viroplasms, but is also incompetent in promoting the formation of stable RNA-RNA contacts between segmental ssRNAs.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research and the authors' own FCCS data.

claim: RV ssRNAs do not form higher order species in vitro without NSP2 or heat-annealing.
source: Using the FCCS-based approach, we did not detect inter-segment interactions prior the incubation with NSP2, consistent with previously reported lack of association of the RNAs, emerging from the transcribing rotavirions (Periz et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by FCCS data and citation to previous research.

claim: Both NSP2 and NSP5 are capable of binding short ssRNA with nanomolar affinity.
source: Both NSP2 and NSP5 were capable of binding a short 18-nt long ssRNA with nM affinity, yielding the apparent hydrodynamic radii, Rh, closely matching the sizes of NSP2 octamers (Schuck et al., 2001), or NSP5 decamers (Martin et al., 2011), respectively (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by FCS data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A and citations.

claim: NSP2 octamers can bind two differently labeled ssRNAs simultaneously.
source: The non-zero CCF (blue circles) suggest that both differently labelled RNAs may bind a single NSP2 octamer with high affinity, consistent with the previously reported binding of two 20-mer RNAs per single NSP2 octamer (Schuck et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by FCCS data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4A and citation.

claim: The apparent hydrodynamic radius of S11 RNA is approximately 9 nm after heat-annealing.
source: The S11 ssRNA, after heat annealing, has a smaller hydrodynamic radius (Rh ~ 8 nm) compared to non-heat treated RNA (~13 nm).
evidence: This claim is supported by FCS measurements described in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D.

claim: Prolonged incubation of S11 RNA in the presence of 10 mM Mg2+ leads to RNA oligomerization.
source: A prolonged incubation of s11 RNA in the presence of 10 mM Mg2+ leads to an increase of Rh, indicating RNA oligomerization.
evidence: This claim is supported by FCS data described in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D.

claim: The apparent hydrodynamic radius of NSP2-bound S11 and S10 RNAs is approximately 30 nm.
source: Analysis of the resulting ACFs and the CCF confirms that both NSP2-bound RNAs have similar hydrodynamic radii, Rh ~30 nm, significantly larger than the protein-free S11 and S10 ssRNAs (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by FCCS analysis data referenced in Supplementary file 1.

claim: The apparent CCF amplitudes between S11 and other segment RNAs are not proportional to the length or size of the interacting RNA partner.
source: The apparent CCF amplitudes between S11 and any other segment RNA are not proportional to the length or the size of the interacting RNA partner (Supplementary file 1), suggesting that it is the RNA sequence, rather than its size, that is important for S11 binding.
evidence: This claim is inferred from FCCS data analysis comparing CCF amplitudes with RNA sizes.

claim: Omitting S1-S9 RNAs from the reaction significantly decreases the apparent CCF amplitude between S11 and S10 RNAs.
source: Omitting S1-S9 RNAs from the reaction significantly decreased the apparent CCF amplitude between S11 and S10 RNAs (Figure 1, cf. panels A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of FCCS data shown in Figure 1A and 1B.

claim: The S11:S10 interaction involves additional RNAs that may be required to form a larger supramolecular complex.
source: This result suggests that the observed S11:S10 interaction involves additional RNAs that may be required to form a larger supramolecular complex (Trask et al., 2012; Gavazzi et al., 2013a; Gavazzi et al., 2013b).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that omitting S1-S9 reduces S11:S10 interaction, and is supported by citations.

claim: RNA-RNA SELEX can identify multiple RNA-binding sites present in S11 RNA.
source: Analysis of the recovered sequences allows identification of multiple RNA-binding sites present in S11 RNA.
evidence: This claim is supported by the RNA-RNA SELEX methodology and results shown in Figure 2.

claim: The majority of newly formed RNA-binding sites in S11 upon NSP2 binding are located near loop regions and helical junctions.
source: Interestingly, the majority of the newly formed RNA-binding sites were located near the loop regions and helical junctions of the RNA (Figure 2C), potentially reflecting the sites of preferential binding of NSP2 to S11 RNA.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-RNA SELEX data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: There is a positive correlation between the abundance of S11-interacting sequences in S1-S10 and the respective CCF amplitudes.
source: There is a positive correlation between the abundance of S11-interacting sequences present in S1-S10 and the respective CCF amplitudes (Figure 1B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The identified sequence within S10 RNA (region 272-288) is sequestered and has low accessibility for base-pairing with S11 RNA in the presence of NSP2.
source: No significant cross-correlation between S10 and a complementary RNA sequence was observed after incubation with NSP2 (Figure 3—figure supplement 3). In contrast, heat-annealing of a mixture of the two RNAs resulted in a high CCF amplitude (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B and C). This result strongly suggests that the identified sequence within S10 RNA is sequestered, and the free energy change of opening the intramolecular base pairs by NSP2 binding is too high.
evidence: This claim is supported by FCCS data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: The estimated melting temperature of the identified RNA-RNA duplex between S5 and S11 is 46°C.
source: This value is in good agreement with the Tm of the identified RNA-RNA duplex, formed between S5 and S11 (Figure 3, inset, Tm = 46°C, calculated as described in Materials and methods).
evidence: This claim is supported by thermodynamic calculations based on the identified duplex sequence.

claim: Fluorescence correlation spectroscopy allows probing of RNA interactions in extremely dilute solutions, effectively eliminating self-association and aggregation.
source: Unlike most ensemble methods previously used for detecting inter-segment interactions in segmented RNA viruses (Gavazzi et al., 2013b; Fajardo et al., 2015; Fournier et al., 2012), fluorescence correlation spectroscopy (FCS) allows probing of such interactions in extremely dilute solutions, effectively eliminating self-association and aggregation of RNAs (Borodavka et al., 2012; Borodavka et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research and describes a methodological advantage.

claim: PIE-FCCS removes the influence of spectral crosstalk and greatly enhances both sensitivity and specificity.
source: When using pulsed interleaved excitation (PIE) in combination with the high temporal resolution of time-correlated single photon counting (TCSPC), the signals can be further divided by the excitation source. This removes the influence of the crosstalk and greatly enhances both the sensitivity and specificity of this technique (Müller et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research describing the PIE-FCCS technique.

claim: The stabilities of identified inter-segment RNA-RNA duplexes correlate well with the apparent CCF amplitudes.
source: Overall, the stabilities of the identified inter-segment RNA-RNA duplexes correlate well with the apparent CCF amplitudes.
evidence: This claim is a conclusion drawn from comparing thermodynamic calculations with FCCS measurements.

claim: The identified sequences demonstrate the importance of specific sequences in the formation of stable and sequence-specific RNA-RNA contacts between S5 and S11.
source: Collectively, these data demonstrate the importance of the identified sequences in the formation of stable and sequence-specific RNA-RNA contacts between S5 and S11.
evidence: This claim is a conclusion drawn from mutagenesis and complementation experiments.

claim: The experimental framework combining PIE-FCCS and RNA-RNA SELEX offers unprecedented capacity for detection of stable, sequence-specific interactions between labeled RNAs in complex mixtures.
source: Such assays offer unprecedented capacity for detection of stable, sequence-specific interactions between labeled RNAs in complex mixtures of RNAs and proteins.
evidence: This claim describes the capabilities of the developed methodology.

claim: RV ssRNAs can specifically interact with each other as a result of RNA remodeling brought about by NSP2.
source: The data presented here collectively support the model in which RV ssRNAs can specifically interact with each other as a result of RNA remodeling brought about by the ssRNA-binding protein NSP2 (Figure 5).
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by all experimental data.

claim: NSP2 may remain associated with the oligomeric ssRNA complex prior to its replication.
source: Because of the high affinity of NSP2 for ssRNA it is expected that NSP2 may remain associated with the oligomeric ssRNA complex prior its replication.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on the known high affinity of NSP2 for ssRNA.

claim: VP2 binding to the ssRNA-NSP2 complex may result in displacement of NSP2 during core assembly.
source: Given that NSP2 inhibits the initiation of replication, but not the elongation stage (Vende et al., 2003), it is possible that the inner core protein VP2 binding to the ssRNA-NSP2 complex (Guglielmi et al., 2010; Estrozi et al., 2013; Patton, 1996) would result in the initial displacement of the NSP2 during the core assembly nucleation, followed by further eviction of NSP2 during the elongation.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on citations to previous research and the authors' model.

claim: The proposed model accounts for incorporation of multiple assorted (+)ssRNAs, each associated with its own copy of the VP1 polymerase.
source: The proposed model would account for incorporation of multiple assorted (+)ssRNAs, each associated with its own copy of the VP1 polymerase (Guglielmi et al., 2010; Patton, 1996; Periz et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is part of the proposed model, supported by citations to previous research.

claim: VP2 nucleation must be tightly regulated to prevent early assembly and ensure specific packaging of eleven (+)ssRNAs.
source: This implies that VP2 nucleation must be tightly regulated to prevent early assembly to ensure specific packaging of eleven (+)ssRNAs (Desselberger et al., 2013; Viskovska et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that VP2 can self-assemble into empty particles, and is supported by citations.

claim: Nucleation of core assembly by (+)ssRNA complexes may occur at VP2 concentrations significantly lower than those required for formation of empty cores.
source: It is possible that nucleation of core assembly by (+)ssRNA complexes may occur at VP2 concentrations significantly lower, than those required for formation of empty cores (Borodavka et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on citation to previous research.

claim: Binding of NSP2 may contribute to regulation of over-nucleation of VP2 on the RNA substrate.
source: Binding of NSP2 may also contribute to the regulation of over-nucleation of VP2 on the RNA substrate (Viskovska et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on citation to previous research.

claim: Early biochemical studies suggest that (+)ssRNA replication may take place within pre-core intermediates lacking a complete VP2 shell.
source: Early biochemical studies of RV assembly intermediates suggest that (+)ssRNA replication may take place within the pre-core intermediates lacking a complete VP2 shell (Gallegos and Patton, 1989).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: The proposed model explains the absence of NSP2 inside assembled virions despite its abundance in viroplasms.
source: The proposed model would explain the absence of NSP2 inside the assembled virions, despite its abundance in viroplasms and high affinity for ssRNAs (Figure 5).
evidence: This claim is part of the proposed model, explaining an observed phenomenon.

claim: In Bluetongue virus, multiple sites of the smallest segment S10 RNA are involved in assortment of other genomic segments.
source: In BTV, multiple sites of the smallest segment S10 RNA have been shown to be involved in assortment of other genomic segments (Fajardo et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research on BTV.

claim: In influenza A viruses, genome segment packaging is coordinated via interactions among different viral RNA segments.
source: In IAVs, genome segment packaging into virions is coordinated via interactions among the different viral RNA segments, while the sites of inter-segment interactions overlap with the coding regions of segmental RNAs (Gavazzi et al., 2013b; Gerber et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on IAV.

claim: The IAV nucleoprotein regulates selective packaging of viral genomic segments.
source: The IAV nucleoprotein (NP) has also been shown to regulate selective packaging of the viral genomic segments (Moreira et al., 2016), revealing the distinct amino acid residues of NP that are required for packaging of specific RNA segments.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research on IAV.

claim: IAV segment ssRNAs form higher order species in vitro only upon co-incubation at 55°C.
source: Interestingly, the IAV segment ssRNAs were shown to form higher order species in vitro; however most of these interactions were only detectable upon co-incubation of the RNAs at 55°C (Gavazzi et al., 2013a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research on IAV.

claim: BTV ssRNAs interact with each other with extremely low efficiencies unless they were co-transcribed in vitro.
source: Similarly, BTV ssRNAs would also interact with each other, albeit with extremely low efficiencies, unless they were co-transcribed in vitro (Fajardo et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research on BTV.

claim: The combination of FCCS and RNA-RNA SELEX holds promise for validation and quantitative analyses of interacting viral ssRNAs and miRNAs.
source: The combination of FCCS and RNA-RNA SELEX-based approaches holds promise for validation and quantitative analyses of the interacting viral ssRNAs and miRNAs.
evidence: This claim describes the potential applications of the developed methodology.

claim: The developed methods will become useful tools for gaining novel mechanistic insights into the dynamics of genomic RNA-RNA interactions in RNA viruses.
source: We anticipate that these methods will become useful tools in the armory of instruments for gaining novel mechanistic insights into the dynamics of genomic RNA-RNA interactions in RNA viruses.
evidence: This claim describes the anticipated impact of the developed methodology.
